title: Is there a pharmacy nearby?
goal: Use the two most frequent words in all of Bulgarian — **има** and **няма** — to talk about having and about existence, and see that one word covers both English "has" and "there is".
bekal: say what you have and don't have
say where things are with seven place prepositions

dialogs.title: Диалог — Asking in the street
dialogs.intro: Ani stops on the sidewalk and asks a passer-by. Count how many times **има** and **няма** come up — and notice that they don't always mean the same thing.

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.id: Excuse me, is there a pharmacy nearby?

lines.speaker: Минувач:
lines.id: Yes, there is. Over there, next to the bank.
lines.literal: yes, there-is. here-is — there, next-to — bank-the.

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.id: And an ATM? I only have big notes.
lines.literal: and — ATM? have-I — only — big — banknotes.

lines.speaker: Минувач:
lines.id: There's no ATM here. There's one in the mall.
lines.literal: ATM — there-isn't — here. there-is — in — mall-the.

lines.speaker: Минувач:
lines.id: No, ten minutes on foot. Do you have a map?
lines.literal: no, ten — minutes — on-foot. have-you-(formal) — (question) — map?

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.id: I have a phone, but I don't have internet.

lines.speaker: Минувач:
lines.id: No problem. Go straight ahead and then turn right.
lines.literal: there-isn't — problem. walk-(formal) — straight — and — then — to-the-right.

lines.speaker: Минувач:
lines.id: You're welcome. Have a nice day!

notes: **Има has two jobs.** As an ordinary verb it means "has": *Той има кола* — he has a car. With no subject it means "there is / there are": *Има кола* — there's a car. The only difference is whether there's a subject in front. Spanish *hay* and French *il y a* work in a similar way — one word where English needs "there is".
**Няма is one word for "there isn't", not two.** Bulgarian doesn't say *не има*; that combination has fused into *няма*. The same goes for "I don't have": not *не имам* but **нямам**.

⚠️ **After има and няма, the noun does NOT take the article.** *Има аптека* — there's a pharmacy (some pharmacy). If you add the article — *Има аптеката* — the sentence sounds odd, because *има*'s job is to introduce something new. Once the thing is known, you switch to *е*: *Аптеката е там.* English does the same: "there's **a** pharmacy", not "there's the pharmacy".

**Има and няма never change form when they mean "there is".** One thing or a thousand, male or female: *Има човек* (there's a person), *Има хора* (there are people). Compare English, which demands *there is* and *there are*.

**Няма защо literally means "there's nothing to (thank me) for" and it's "you're welcome".** It's the most common answer to *благодаря*, a bit warmer than *моля*. If you only learn one, learn this one.
**Няма проблем has become an everyday phrase** and is used exactly like English "no problem". You'll hear it dozens of times a day.

**Само means "only", and it goes right in front of the word it limits.** *Имам само телефон* (I only have a phone) is different from *Само аз имам телефон* (only I have a phone). Moving *само* moves the whole meaning of the sentence.
**Пеша means "on foot" and never changes.** *Десет минути пеша* — ten minutes on foot. You'll hear it a lot in Sofia, a city most of which you can cover by walking.

grammars.title: Имам and нямам — have and don't have
body: This verb belongs to Group III, the most regular and the biggest verb group in Bulgarian. Learn the six forms below and you've learned the pattern for hundreds of other verbs.
after: Notice that the negative isn't *не* + verb, but a separate word whose first letters change: **и- → ня-**. This is the only Bulgarian verb that behaves this way, so there's no other pattern to worry about.

grammars.title: Има / няма with no subject — "there is" and "there isn't"
body: In their second job, the forms freeze in the third person singular and never change. Only the noun that follows changes.

sections.title: Seven place prepositions that cover almost everything

blocks.text: Because Bulgarian nouns don't change form, the preposition is the only thing you need to choose correctly — the noun just goes after it as it is. Compare Russian, where every preposition demands a different form of the noun.

head: Preposition
Say it
Meaning
Example
rows: до банката — next to the bank
пред хотела — in front of the hotel

blocks.text: ⚠️ The difference between **в** and **на** is the only one that needs practice. **В** means being *inside* something with space: *в стаята, в България, в колата*. **На** means being *on a surface* or *at a place of activity*: *на масата* (on the table), *на работа* (at work), *на море* (at the sea, meaning on a beach holiday).

The form **във** is used only when the next word begins with **в** or **ф** — *във Варна*, *във Франция* — so you don't trip over the sounds. The same rule gives **със** instead of **с**: *със сестра ми*.

sections.title: Има and няма in everyday phrases

blocks.text: The last row shows something typical: **няма** can take a short pronoun to say that someone isn't there. *Няма го* — he isn't here. *Няма я* — she isn't here. *Няма ме* — I'm not around. You'll hear it often in offices and on the phone.

items: There are a lot of people.
